chapter_theme: Neelakesi reaches Ulokan, the follower of Kanada, who sets out the Vaisheshika's six categories and nine substances; she answers that the four elements are one stuff changing into each other, that sound does not prove ether, that direction is space named relative to an observer, that mind and time are not single substances, and that qualities cannot be separate from their bearer nor joined to it by inherence, offering at the end the Jain triad of arising, perishing and lasting.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Vaisheshika ascetic, follower of Kanada (கணாதன்), whom Neelakesi debates in the வைசேடிக வாதச் சருக்கம்

783.reading: Having won over the previous opponent as well, Neelakesi goes on and, among the many ancients who taught their ways as the path to release, reaches the place of Ulokan, who had stored up the teaching that Kanada is the master.
783.nuance: The sarukkam opens by naming Kanada (கணாதன்) as the founder whose teaching the opponent holds; the opponent himself is called உலோகன், a name that recalls the school's other title for its founder, though the verse uses it of the debater. The word division of line 4 (ஈட்டினான் உலோகனது இடத்தை) is the reading assumed here.
783.event: Neelakesi, having converted her last opponent, travels on to the dwelling of Ulokan, the follower of Kanada.

784.reading: The great ascetic sees the beautiful woman, takes her for one come in a contentious mood, and tells her to listen while he sets out, for her to take to heart, the truth that stands on the right path.
784.event: Ulokan sees Neelakesi, judges her ready to argue, and offers to expound his doctrine.

785.reading: The Vaisheshika says the path is the abiding truth, and that the categories, hard to know, are six: substance, quality, action, the general, the particular, and the joining of them.
785.nuance: The six are given in Tamil and Sanskrit mixed: திரப்பியம் for substance, குணம், தொழில், then பொது and சிறப்பு, and inherence only as the act of joining (புணர்ப்பது). Neelakesi answers the substances in 791 to 797 and the separation of quality from substance and the joining in 798 to 802.

claims.claim: reality is set out in six categories: substance, quality, action, generality, particularity and inherence

786.reading: He names the substances as nine, the five elements with direction, mind, time and soul; qualities are their nature, and action is the moving of the substances from place to place.
786.nuance: Action is defined as புடைபெயர்ச்சி, shifting position, so action is motion only. Each of the nine is attacked in turn from 791: the elements, ether (793), direction (794 to 796), mind and time (797).

claims.claim: there are nine substances: five elements, direction, mind, time and soul
action is the movement of a substance

787.reading: He defines the general as the higher and lower sameness that gathers things into their kinds, the particular as what makes a thing known as distinct, and the joining as what lets one say that these qualities and actions belong to this thing.
787.nuance: The joining is defined by what it licenses one to say (கிளத்தல், line 4), and that is where Neelakesi presses in 800 to 802: if a quality is other than its bearer, nothing makes it 'its'.

claims.claim: generality, higher and lower, gathers things into classes and particularity marks each as distinct
inherence is what makes qualities and actions belong to their substance

788.reading: The narrator sums up: the Vaisheshika taught that of the six the first three have being and the last three do not, and that substances, qualities and actions are each separate from one another.
788.nuance: The verse says the last three reached இன்மை, non-being; this is the Jain poem's wording, and the school would more likely say that generality, particularity and inherence lack the universal of being rather than that they do not exist. The separateness of substance, quality and action is the claim the rest of the chapter attacks (798 to 802).

claims.claim: of the six categories the first three possess being and the last three do not
substance, quality and action are separate from each other

789.reading: When he lifts his head and asks whether these principles are not right, Neelakesi answers that to practise penance on such principles would be false penance, and she will go.
789.nuance: The verse runs his question and her answer together; the division assumed here gives lines 1 and 2 (to ஒத்ததன்றோ, with உரை நல்லாய் as his address to her) to him and lines 3 and 4 to her.
789.event: Ulokan asks proudly whether his principles are not sound; Neelakesi says penance on them is false and makes to leave.

claims.claim: penance founded on the Vaisheshika principles is false penance

790.reading: He tells her that since she heard him expound the true path and calls it unsound, she must prove it a false path before she leaves; she stops him with a raised hand and bids him listen while she shows it.
790.event: Ulokan challenges Neelakesi to prove his doctrine false before leaving, and she halts him and begins her refutation.

791.reading: Neelakesi says the four elements from earth onward are one if their origin and form are considered, though he recites them as separate primary substances, and offers to show how they pass into one another in either order.
791.nuance: Her point is that the four are not four kinds of stuff but one stuff in four states, which turn into each other forwards and backwards (வலமுறை இடமுறை); the examples follow in 792.

claims.claim: earth, water, fire and air are four distinct substances
the four elements are of one kind and change into one another

792.reading: She gives examples of the elements turning into one another: water joined to the right thing becomes salt, ghee blazes up as fire, wind roars from agitation, and a great hailstone is a lump of water that came from water layer by layer.
792.nuance: Each example is a change across the Vaisheshika's boundaries between elements: water to earthy salt, a liquid to fire, water to a solid. Line 3 was repaired in the text (see source_issues) and the details of lines 2 and 3 are uncertain.

claims.claim: one element is seen to turn into another, as water into salt and into hail

793.reading: She says that since he makes sound the quality of ether, and no element stands firm on its own or is joined with sound among the primary ones, he should give up the clamour of his ether.
793.nuance: What she dismisses is 'your' ether (நின் காயம்), the one defined by sound; in 794 she herself folds direction into space (காயம்), so the attack is on the Vaisheshika's proof of ether, not on space as such. Line 3 is obscure and the middle of the argument is uncertain.

claims.claim: sound is the quality of ether
sound gives no ground for positing the Vaisheshika's ether

794.reading: She says direction is only pointing: from where the sun set and rose people make four, eight or many quarters and use them by convention, and even so it comes down to space.

claims.claim: direction is space named by convention from the sun's rising and setting, not a substance of its own

795.reading: She proposes setting many people in a circle with one in the middle and asking him to name the directions: if the eight directions are born from where he stands, she sees no thing of his called direction, and asks him to show it.
795.nuance: The thought experiment makes direction relative to an observer: the same spot is a different quarter for each person in the ring.

claims.claim: the directions arise relative to an observer, so no substance called direction is ever seen

796.reading: She says that if a quarter is that direction for one person and not for another, and people at every point can say the same, he should go, now devoted, and live holding the feet of the Supreme as attainment and the end.
796.nuance: The verse closes the case on direction with an appeal to conversion; the Supreme (பரமன்) is in the Jain poem the Arhat. The syntax of lines 2 and 3 (ஏக நீ, இனி என்னை) is uncertain.

claims.claim: a direction is one quarter for one person and another for the next, so it has no nature of its own
the feet of the Supreme are attainment and the final end

797.reading: She says what is called mind is the union of the soul with bodily form, and that time is of two kinds, so his time does not stand as a substance there.
797.nuance: She does not deny mind or time outright: mind is placed in the soul's union with the body, and time is split in two (இருமைத்து), against the Vaisheshika's single substance. What the two kinds are the verse does not say.

claims.claim: mind is the soul joined with bodily form, not a separate substance
time is twofold, so it is not a single substance

798.reading: She asks that if qualities and actions are other than their substance, how a corpse ever came to be a living soul; if the soul in itself neither knows nor speaks, nothing ever reached it and we were never joined to it.
798.nuance: The target is the separation of knowing from the knower: if awareness is only a quality added to the soul, the soul by itself is as inert as a corpse.

claims.claim: qualities and actions are other than the substance that has them
a soul without knowing of its own would be no different from a corpse

799.reading: She argues that if a thing has no quality of its own, it is other than any quality, and as surely as fire cannot be shown by its coldness, such things would never appear at all.
799.nuance: The simile of line 3 (fire and cold in a vessel) is compressed and its exact turn uncertain.

claims.claim: a thing taken apart from its qualities could never appear

800.reading: She says that if, having called quality and bearer separate, he needs a further thing to join them, that is false: since quality and bearer have no joining apart from each other, neither can be made known and neither exists.
800.nuance: This is the answer to the joining of 787: a link between two things that are never apart is either needless or, if they are truly apart, unable to make either known.

claims.claim: a separate inherence is needed to join qualities to their bearers
quality and bearer need no third thing to join them, and taken apart neither exists

801.reading: She says the nine substances are many by their own being, and that their number, their hardness and each quality are known only because they belong to the thing.
801.nuance: The verse could also be read as the Vaisheshika's reply that qualities are known through their relation of belonging; the reading here takes it as Neelakesi's, leading into 802.

claims.claim: a thing's number and qualities are known only as belonging to it

802.reading: She asks how, if a thing's quality is other than it, he can slip into calling it this thing's quality; and if the soul is one thing without knowing, it could not even suffer, and that would have to be true.
802.nuance: Line 3's உதனமு is obscure; the reading of lines 3 and 4 as an absurd consequence (no knowing, so no suffering) is a guess.

claims.claim: a quality other than its thing cannot be called that thing's quality

803.reading: She says that if he grants that a thing perishes when its state perishes, then destruction is admitted, and there is nothing to regret: if he also admits its arising and takes in the three together, that would be very fine.
803.nuance: The three (மும்மை) are arising, perishing and lasting, the Jain triad she set out against Mokkalan (387). Here she offers it as the settlement for a school that held the substances eternal.

claims.claim: every real thing has arising, perishing and lasting together

links.note: The Manimekalai's Vaisheshika gives the same six categories (பொருள், குணம், கருமம், சாமானியம், விசேடம், கூட்டம்) and is left unanswered; Neelakesi's opponent gives them in 785 to 788 and she answers them from 791.
links.teaches: The six-category list was a fixed set piece of Tamil accounts of the schools, and the two epics differ in what they do with it: the Buddhist epic records it and moves on, the Jain epic makes each category a target.

links.note: The Manimekalai's Jain counts space (ஆகாயம்) as a substance that gives room to all things; in 794 Neelakesi says the Vaisheshika's direction comes down to space.
links.teaches: Neelakesi's denial of direction is not a denial of space: the Jain list keeps space as a substance, so she can fold direction into it rather than abolish it.

links.note: In 387 Neelakesi gives Mokkalan the threefold nature of arising, perishing and lasting; in 803 she offers the same three to the Vaisheshika.
links.teaches: The one triad is aimed at opposite errors: against the Buddhist it adds lasting to momentary things, against the Vaisheshika it adds perishing to eternal substances.

links.note: The Manimekalai's Jain says each thing is both lasting and passing and has arising, staying and perishing (தோற்றமும் நிலையும் கேடும்); 803 names the three as மும்மை.
links.teaches: A Buddhist epic's report and a Jain epic's own argument agree on the triad as the Jain signature, which shows the Buddhist account of this doctrine is faithful where the Jain uses it.

links.note: In 393 Neelakesi tells the Buddhist that quality and bearer are both different and one; in 800 she tells the Vaisheshika that they need no third thing to join them.
links.teaches: Her 'different and one' answers two opposite opponents: the Buddhist who keeps qualities without a bearer, and the Vaisheshika who keeps a bearer so apart from its qualities that it needs a joining category.

links.note: In 499 she tells the Buddhist that nothing is ever known except through its qualities; in 802 she tells the Vaisheshika that a quality other than its thing cannot be called its.
links.teaches: The same principle that a thing is reached only through its qualities is used first to prove a bearer exists and then to deny that the bearer can stand apart from what it bears.

new_concepts.gloss: formal debate between schools, opened by a challenge and held before a king's assembly
new_concepts.label_source: the sarukkam's rubric (வைசேடிக வாதச் சருக்கம்); id as declared in neelakesi ch008, since vaadham is taken

new_concepts.gloss: a quality of a thing, lasting or passing, and its relation to the substance (பொருள், குணி) that bears it
new_concepts.label_source: the verses' own word: குணம் (785, 793, 798, 799, 801, 802), குணி (800); id as declared in neelakesi ch018

new_concepts.gloss: transformation: a substance passing into new modes, as milk into curd, while something of it persists
new_concepts.label_source: declared in neelakesi ch018 from பரிணாமத்திரிவு (386); here the elements passing into one another (791) and the triad (803)

source_issues: 783 line 4: the run மீட்டினா னுலோகன திடத்தை is read as ஈட்டினான் உலோகனது இடத்தை; the opponent's name rests on this division.
792 line 3: the text was repaired from a TSCII leftover (flagged by show); the line's sense is uncertain.
793 line 3 (ஒலியொடு முதறம்முட் புல்லல்) is obscure, probably corrupt.
802 line 3: உதனமு is not a word I can identify; possibly corrupt.
803 line 2: மதற்குநி is read as அதற்கு நீ.
